original_question: Let X be a hyperkahler manifold of dimension 2r. If L is a nontrivial nef line bundle on X with Beauville-Bogomolov square q(L) = 0, determine whether there must exist a Lagrangian fibration f: X -> P^r such that L = f^* O_{P^r}(k) for some integer k >= 1. More generally, determine whether X is birational to a hyperkahler manifold X' admitting a Lagrangian fibration X' -> P^r exactly when X carries a nontrivial line bundle L with q(L) = 0.
target_in_paper: In the arXiv v1 PDF, the draft is targeting Section 1.6, Conjecture 2(a)-(b) on Lagrangian fibrations, introduced immediately after Proposition 3 as its higher-dimensional generalization and read in the context of Theorem 4.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the precise mathematical core of Beauville's conjecture: X has complex dimension 2r; the first clause assumes a nontrivial nef line bundle L with Beauville-Bogomolov square q(L)=0; the expected conclusion is a Lagrangian fibration X -> P^r with L pulled back from O_{P^r}(k) for some k >= 1; and the second clause asks for a birational/bimeromorphic criterion in terms of the existence of a nontrivial isotropic line bundle. The draft also correctly keeps the base as P^r rather than an arbitrary lower-dimensional manifold.
missing_details: The paper works over the complex numbers in the compact Kahler category: a hyperkahler manifold here means a compact, simply connected, irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifold.
The notation q(L) should be made explicit as q(c1(L)), where q: H^2(X,Z) -> Z is the Beauville-Bogomolov quadratic form defined in Section 1.3.
A Lagrangian fibration is defined in Section 1.6 as a proper holomorphic map h: X -> B whose general fiber is connected, has dimension r, and is isotropic for the holomorphic symplectic form.
In part (b), the paper says X' is bimeromorphic to X, not merely birational; this matters because no projectivity assumption is imposed.
The conjecture is stated without assuming X is projective, even though Theorem 4 only proves the base is P^r in the projective case and says the nonprojective extension is expected.
The paper explicitly says it is not clear whether clause (a) implies clause (b) or conversely, so the second clause should not be presented as a proved equivalent reformulation of the first.
The surrounding context is that this is the higher-dimensional analogue of Proposition 3 for K3 surfaces; making that framing explicit keeps the question closer to the paper's intent.
refined_question: Let X be a compact hyperkahler manifold over C (equivalently, an irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifold) of complex dimension 2r, and let q: H^2(X,Z) -> Z be its Beauville-Bogomolov quadratic form. Is the following higher-dimensional analogue of the K3 elliptic-fibration criterion true? (a) If L != O_X is a nef line bundle on X with q(c1(L)) = 0, must there exist a Lagrangian fibration f: X -> P^r such that L is isomorphic to f^*O_{P^r}(k) for some integer k >= 1? (b) More generally, is it true that there exists a hyperkahler manifold X' bimeromorphic to X together with a Lagrangian fibration X' -> P^r if and only if X admits a line bundle L != O_X with q(c1(L)) = 0? Here a Lagrangian fibration means a proper holomorphic map whose general fiber is a connected r-dimensional Lagrangian submanifold for the holomorphic symplectic form.
justification: The draft is very close to the exact target statement. In the arXiv version of the paper, Beauville states this in Section 1.6 as Conjecture 2(a)-(b), immediately after Proposition 3 on K3 surfaces and after Theorem 4, which explains why a nontrivial fibration from a hyperkahler manifold should be Lagrangian and, in the projective case, have base P^r. Sections 1.1 and 1.3 provide the hidden setup your draft leaves implicit: the complex compact Kahler meaning of 'hyperkahler manifold' and the definition of the Beauville-Bogomolov form q. The main corrections needed for full paper-faithfulness are to spell out q(c1(L)), replace 'birational' by 'bimeromorphic', define 'Lagrangian fibration', and avoid suggesting that parts (a) and (b) are known to be equivalent, since Beauville explicitly says this is unclear.
